Family Health

Bleeding haemorrhoids: assessment, relief and treatment choices

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Seeing blood after a bowel movement can be frightening. Haemorrhoids, also called piles, are one possible cause, but the appearance of the blood cannot establish the diagnosis. A useful plan starts with checking the bleeding, then choosing care that eases symptoms and makes passing stool less difficult.

Internal, external and thrombosed haemorrhoids are different

Haemorrhoids are enlarged vascular cushions in the lower rectum or around the anus. Internal ones may bleed without pain or protrude during a bowel movement. External ones are covered by sensitive skin and can cause itching, tenderness or a noticeable lump.

A clot inside an external haemorrhoid can produce a suddenly painful, firm swelling. The skin over it may break and bleed. Do not cut, squeeze or drain it yourself: a clinician needs to confirm what the lump is and decide whether conservative care or a procedure is appropriate.

Why bleeding happens, and why it still needs checking

Hard stool and straining can injure fragile tissue, leaving bright red blood on paper, on the stool or in the toilet. Irritation, protruding tissue and breakdown over a clot can also contribute. The amount and persistence of bleeding matter more than deciding at home exactly which mechanism caused it.

An anal fissure, bowel inflammation, a polyp or another bowel condition can cause a similar symptom. A known haemorrhoid does not exclude a second cause. Do not assume that blood is harmless because it is bright red, painless or similar to an earlier episode.

When to seek immediate or prompt help

Get emergency help for bleeding that does not stop, a large amount of blood, large clots, faintness or collapse. Severe pain with bleeding also needs urgent assessment. Black or dark-red stool, bloody diarrhoea, fever, pus or feeling very unwell warrants urgent medical advice.

Seek prompt advice for unexplained or painless rectal bleeding, repeated episodes or a changed pattern, even when the amount seems small. Mention weight loss, unusual tiredness and persistent bowel changes. Do not wait a week for home care to work when bleeding is substantial.

Prepare a useful account of what has changed

Note when bleeding began, whether it occurs with bowel movements, its colour and approximate amount, and whether there is pain, a lump or tissue coming out. Explain changes in stool consistency, frequency, abdominal discomfort, nausea or vomiting.

Bring a medicine list, including aspirin, anticoagulants, supplements and treatments already tried. A primary-care clinician can arrange examination and decide whether gastroenterology or colorectal assessment is needed. Do not stop a prescribed medicine affecting clotting without instructions from the treating team.

Examination and further tests depend on the findings

Assessment may include looking at the anal area, a gloved-finger rectal examination and a short viewing instrument to examine the anal canal. Ask what each step is for, and request a pause or chaperone if that helps you feel comfortable.

Some people need further bowel investigation, including colonoscopy. Reasons can include no clear bleeding source, associated bowel or abdominal symptoms, continued bleeding after treatment, family history or being due for screening. Not everyone needs the same tests, but finding piles should not end an investigation when other features remain unexplained.

Make stools easier to pass without unnecessary food bans

Increase fibre gradually through fruit, vegetables, beans and whole grains, alongside an amount of fluid appropriate for your health. If you have a prescribed fluid restriction, ask how to balance it with bowel care. Sudden large increases in fibre can make bloating harder to manage.

There is no general requirement to remove all dairy, meat, white bread or frozen foods. Some choices contain little fibre and may need balancing with others; frozen vegetables, for example, are not equivalent to every processed meal. A restrictive elimination diet is not a standard treatment for piles.

Fibre supplements and laxatives have a separate role

A pharmacist or clinician may suggest a fibre supplement such as psyllium or methylcellulose when food changes are insufficient. A stool-softening or osmotic laxative may be appropriate in other circumstances. These options address constipation; a local haemorrhoid cream does not soften stool.

Polyethylene glycol is one osmotic option that helps retain water in stool. Response can take several days and varies by product and person. Follow the label and professional advice rather than combining products or expecting a guaranteed result within one to three days. Vomiting, marked swelling or possible bowel blockage needs assessment before self-treatment. Ask about suitability in pregnancy or breastfeeding.

Change toilet habits and keep movement manageable

Respond to the urge to open your bowels, avoid forceful straining and leave the toilet when finished. Reading or scrolling can prolong pressure on the area. Fifteen minutes should not become a target or permitted sitting allowance.

Regular activity can support bowel habits. If heavy lifting repeatedly worsens symptoms, discuss technique and temporary adjustments; avoiding every shopping bag or ordinary movement is unnecessary. Comfortable clothing and breathable underwear may reduce rubbing, but they are not a treatment for the underlying vascular tissue.

Use gentle measures for local comfort

A comfortably warm bath may soothe the area. A cold pack wrapped in cloth can provide short periods of relief; do not apply ice directly to skin. Clean gently with water or soft unscented material, then pat dry. A bidet can help if the pressure is gentle, while repeated scrubbing can aggravate soreness.

Epsom salts are not essential to a bath, and added fragrances or remedies may irritate. Witch-hazel products are marketed for discomfort, but evidence is limited and prolonged topical use can cause sensitivity. These measures should never delay assessment of bleeding or replace a confirmed treatment plan.

Choose symptom medicines carefully

Creams, ointments and suppositories can provide temporary relief of itching or discomfort. External and internal preparations are not interchangeable. Follow the directions for the product supplied; hydrocortisone products should generally be limited to seven days unless a clinician advises otherwise.

Have symptoms reviewed if they do not improve or return quickly. Ask about suitable pain relief: codeine can worsen constipation, and NHS advice is to avoid ibuprofen when piles are bleeding. Prescription medicines, other illnesses and pregnancy can change which option is suitable.

Banding is a professional treatment for internal piles

For continuing internal symptoms, a clinician may place a small band around haemorrhoidal tissue to cut off its blood supply. The treated tissue subsequently separates and the area heals. This is performed in the appropriate internal location, not as a home method for an external lump.

A person may need more than one treatment. Ask about discomfort, delayed bleeding and aftercare before leaving. The timing of tissue separation and recovery is not a guarantee; new heavy bleeding, severe pain, fever or difficulty urinating after treatment needs urgent assessment.

Injection and coagulation are other office options

Injection treatment, or sclerotherapy, uses a solution that produces scarring and shrinks the affected tissue. Coagulation techniques use energy, such as infrared light or an electrical current, to achieve a similar treatment goal. Repeat sessions may be needed.

You may also hear about bipolar and laser techniques. A device name does not establish that a procedure is suitable, superior or available locally. Discuss the type of haemorrhoid, expected benefit, discomfort, recurrence and alternatives with the clinician rather than choosing by a promised one- or two-week result.

Surgery is considered when less invasive care is insufficient

Large external haemorrhoids, significant prolapse or persistent symptoms can lead to a discussion about surgery. Haemorrhoidectomy removes affected tissue. The decision considers the problem’s extent and effect on daily life, previous treatment and the person’s health.

Ask about the anaesthetic, pain relief, bowel-care plan and time away from usual activities. Some operations are day cases and others require a longer stay. Do not automatically begin suppositories before surgery: preparation and aftercare must come from the team performing the procedure.

Artery ligation and stapled surgery involve different trade-offs

Haemorrhoidal artery ligation uses sutures to reduce blood supply, sometimes guided by Doppler ultrasound and combined with a repair for prolapse. Compared with excision it may involve less pain, but recurrence can be more frequent, particularly with more advanced disease.

Stapled haemorrhoidopexy repositions internal tissue rather than treating external haemorrhoids. ASCRS does not recommend it routinely as the first surgical option because of its effectiveness and risk profile. Ask why the proposed approach fits your anatomy and priorities instead of treating all procedures as interchangeable.

Recovery includes follow-up, not a promise of permanent cure

Many people improve with stool and symptom care, while others need a procedure. Problems can recur even after successful treatment. Continue the agreed bowel plan and report bleeding that persists or returns rather than assuming the original diagnosis explains it indefinitely.

Severe complications such as damaged tissue or major bleeding are not the expected course of every haemorrhoid. At the same time, a painful trapped prolapse, rapidly worsening symptoms or signs of infection should not be managed by extending home treatment. Keep the clinic’s contact details and written aftercare instructions accessible.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Independent patient guidance supports assessment of rectal bleeding, bowel-habit changes and short-term symptom relief. Not every person needs a procedure or colonoscopy.

Surgical guidance distinguishes office treatments and operations according to anatomy, severity, response and risks. A fixed recovery date or a brand name cannot determine the best choice.

How BeMama can help

A brief record of bleeding, bowel symptoms and treatments can help you explain the pattern at an appointment. Tracking does not diagnose the cause or replace an examination.

When to seek help

Do not wait through heavy or continuing bleeding, faintness, collapse or severe pain. Black or dark-red stool, bloody diarrhoea, fever or pus needs urgent advice.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Check the cause of rectal bleeding even when piles seem likely.
  • Use emergency care for heavy or continuing bleeding or collapse.
  • Fibre, suitable fluid and less straining support bowel care.
  • Local creams and constipation medicines serve different purposes.
  • Persistent symptoms need reassessment and sometimes a professional procedure.

Frequently asked questions

Can painless bleeding still need assessment?

Yes. Internal piles may bleed painlessly, but other conditions can do so too. Seek prompt advice rather than using absence of pain as reassurance.

Should I wait a week if there is a lot of blood?

No. Heavy or continuing bleeding requires emergency assessment.

Will haemorrhoid cream treat constipation?

No. Constipation may need dietary measures, a fibre supplement or a separate medicine.

Must I remove all dairy and meat?

No. Focus on a balanced diet with enough fibre unless a clinician has identified a separate reason for avoiding a food.

Are Epsom salts necessary in a sitz bath?

No. Plain comfortably warm water is a reasonable option. Stop products that irritate the skin.

Can I keep using hydrocortisone every week?

Do not repeatedly extend treatment without advice. Symptoms lasting beyond seven days or returning quickly need review.

Should I stop my blood thinner because of bleeding?

Contact the treating clinician promptly. Do not change a prescribed anticoagulant or antiplatelet medicine on your own.

Does everyone need a colonoscopy?

No. The decision depends on the examination, other symptoms, risk factors, previous investigations and screening needs.

Can an external lump be treated with a home band?

No. Banding is a clinician-performed treatment for suitable internal haemorrhoids. Never band, cut or drain a lump yourself.

Can piles return after surgery?

Yes. Recurrence is possible, and new bleeding still needs assessment. Continue the agreed bowel and follow-up plan.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
